facts.text: The applicants are former members of the Turkish National Assembly elected at the general election of 20 October 1991.

anchor.surface_text: 6.  The applicants are former members of the Turkish National Assembly who were elected at the general election of 20 October 1991.

facts.text: The applicants were members of the People’s Labour Party, founded in June 1990 but dissolved by the Constitutional Court on 14 August 1993 for separatist activities.

anchor.surface_text: At that time they were members of the People’s Labour Party (Halkın Emeği Partisi), which was founded in June 1990 but proscribed and dissolved by the Constitutional Court on 14 August 1993 on account of what were held to be separatist activities.

facts.text: By 14 August 1993 the applicants had joined the Democracy Party, which had been set up in the meantime.

anchor.surface_text: By that date the applicants had joined the Democracy Party (Demokrasi Partisi), which had been set up in the meantime.

facts.text: On 2 March 1994 the National Assembly lifted the applicants' parliamentary immunity on an application by the public prosecutor attached to the Ankara National Security Court.

anchor.surface_text: 7.  On 2 March 1994 the National Assembly lifted their parliamentary immunity on an application, first lodged in November 1992 and subsequently resubmitted on several occasions, by the public prosecutor attached to the Ankara National Security Court

facts.text: The public prosecutor accused the applicants of offences defined in Article 125 of the Criminal Code, classified as terrorist crimes under the Prevention of Terrorism Act, within the jurisdiction of national security courts.

anchor.surface_text: He accused them of committing the offences defined in Article 125 of the Criminal Code (see paragraph 20 below), which were classified as terrorist crimes in the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713 – see paragraph 21 below) and thus came within the jurisdiction of the national security courts

facts.text: On 2 March 1994, Mr Dicle and Mr Doğan were arrested on the public prosecutor’s orders as they were leaving the parliament building and taken into police custody at the Ankara security police headquarters.

anchor.surface_text: 8.  On the same day, as they were leaving the parliament building, Mr Dicle and Mr Doğan were arrested on the public prosecutor’s orders and taken into police custody at the headquarters of the anti-terrorist section of the Ankara security police.

facts.text: On 3 March 1994, lawyers for Mr Dicle and Mr Doğan requested their clients be brought promptly before a judge and permission to speak to them, which was granted under supervision for appeal preparation.

anchor.surface_text: On the following day their lawyers asked for their clients to be brought promptly before a judge and asked the publicprosecutor for permission to speak to them. The written authorisation issued by the public prosecutor for that purpose specified that the interview – to be conducted under supervision – was to concern preparation of the appeal the applicants were intending to lodge against the lifting of their parliamentary immunity.

facts.text: The other four applicants refused to leave the parliament precinct but were arrested on 4 March 1994 and taken into police custody.

anchor.surface_text: 9.  The other four applicants had refused to leave the parliament precinct, but on 4 March they suffered the same fate as their two colleagues.

facts.text: On 4 March 1994 the public prosecutor extended the six applicants’ detention in police custody until 16 March 1994 for further investigations, based on section 30 of Law no. 3842.

anchor.surface_text: On that day the public prosecutor extended the six applicants’ detention in police custody until 16 March 1994 on the ground that further investigations were needed; his decision was based on section 30 of Law no. 3842 governing procedure before the national security courts

facts.text: While in police custody, the applicants refused to make any statement.

anchor.surface_text: While in police custody the applicants refused to make any statement.

facts.text: On 11 March 1994, the lawyer for Mr Dicle and Mr Doğan applied again for them to be brought promptly before a judge, citing Articles 5 and 6 of the Convention.

anchor.surface_text: 10.  On 11 March the lawyer acting for Mr Dicle and Mr Doğan, referring to his request of 3 March that they be brought promptly before a judge (see paragraph 8 above), made another application to the same effect, relying on Articles 5 and 6 of the Convention, inter alia.

facts.text: On 21 March 1994 the Constitutional Court dismissed appeals by the applicants against the lifting of their parliamentary immunity.

anchor.surface_text: 11.  On 21 March 1994 the Constitutional Court dismissed appeals lodged by the applicants against the lifting of their parliamentary immunity.

facts.text: On 17 March 1994, a single judge of the National Security Court ordered the applicants’ detention pending trial, citing the nature of the offence and evidence obtained.

anchor.surface_text: 12.  In the meantime, on 17 March 1994, a single judge of the National Security Court had issued an order for the MPs’ detention pending trial, giving as the reasons the “character and nature” of the offence concerned and the “evidence obtained”.

facts.text: On 22 March 1994, a bench of three judges of the National Security Court upheld the detention order on appeal, citing the classification of offences, charges, length of detention, and investigation stage.

anchor.surface_text: 13.  On appeal by the applicants, a bench of three judges of the same court upheld the above order on 22 March 1994, holding that it was necessary “on account of the classification and nature of the offences [concerned], the charges already preferred, the length of [the applicants’] detention and the fact that the case [was] still at the investigation stage”.

facts.text: On 12 April 1994 the applicants applied for release, which was dismissed by the National Security Court on 13 May 1994 as the case was still at the investigation stage and no change had occurred.

anchor.surface_text: 14.  On 12 April the applicants lodged a further application for release, which was dismissed by the National Security Court on 13 May on the ground that the case was “still at the investigation stage” and that to date there had been “no change in the detained MPs’ favour”.

facts.text: On 21 June 1994 the public prosecutor filed submissions accusing the applicants of separatism and undermining State integrity, capital offences under Article 125 of the Criminal Code.

anchor.surface_text: 15.  On 21 June 1994 the public prosecutor filed submissions accusing the applicants of separatism and undermining the integrity of the State, which are capital offences under Article 125 of the Criminal Code (see paragraphs 7 above and 20 below).

facts.text: On 8 December 1994 the National Security Court sentenced Mr Sakık and Mr Alınak to 3.5 years for separatist propaganda and Mr Türk, Mr Dicle, Mr Doğan and Mrs Zana to 15 years for membership of an armed gang.

anchor.surface_text: 16.  On 8 December 1994 the National Security Court delivered its judgment. Applying section 8 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713 – see paragraph 21 below), it sentenced Mr Sakık and Mr Alınak to three years and six months’ imprisonment for separatist propaganda and Mr Türk, Mr Dicle, Mr Doğan and Mrs Zana to fifteen years’ imprisonment for membership of an armed gang (Article 168 of the Criminal Code – see paragraph 20 below).

facts.text: On 26 October 1995 the Court of Cassation quashed Mr Türk’s conviction and ordered his release, upholding other applicants’ convictions.

anchor.surface_text: 17.  On appeal by the applicants and the public prosecutor, the Court of Cassation quashed Mr Türk’s conviction on 26 October 1995 and ordered his release, on the ground that he had contravened section 8 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713) but not Article 168 of the Criminal Code. It upheld the other applicants’ convictions.

facts.text: The applicants were detained in police custody for twelve days (Mr Sakık, Mr Türk, Mr Alınak, Mrs Zana) or fourteen days (Mr Dicle, Mr Doğan) without judicial intervention.

anchor.surface_text: 45.  The Court notes that the applicants’ detention in police custody lasted twelve days in the case of Mr Sakık, Mr Türk, Mr Alınak and Mrs Zana, and fourteen days in the case of Mr Dicle and Mr Doğan.
